title: The Friction Between Centralized and Decentralized Decision-Making
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article frames the tension between centralized and decentralized decision-making as a healthy, ongoing balancing act rather than a problem to solve once and for all. Decentralized, field-level decisions produce speed and practical solutions but risk inconsistency and duplicated effort across the organization. Centralized decisions produce consistency but can bog the enterprise down in bureaucracy and slow response times. The author points to a model used by top-performing organizations, which they call Local Authority and Global Strategy (LAGS): give field leaders authority over day-to-day decisions while keeping strategy and functional oversight centralized. The piece ends by asking readers to locate where their own organization draws that line and whether it's calibrated correctly.
points: Decentralized decision-making produces speed and practical solutions but risks inconsistency and duplicated effort
Centralized decision-making produces consistency but can create costly bureaucracy
The best organizations use a Local Authority, Global Strategy (LAGS) model
Leaders should regularly reassess where the line between local and central authority is drawn
quotes: The tension between making decisions on the ground or in the field as opposed to by a centralized source is a healthy one.
Giving those leaders or producers closest to the issues and problems the ability to make decisions that affect them results in more practical and timely solutions.
The downside of decentralizing decisions is all about consistency and redundancy.
The bureaucracy that gets created to avoid giving too much authority to those on the ground is both costly and highly inefficient.
Local Authority and Global Strategy (LAGS) is the design used by the world’s most effective organizations.
Effective leaders never forget that at the core of organizational life and leadership lies the idea of what to hold onto and what to let go of.
